definitions.definition: Six famous leaders of orders contemporary with the Buddha — Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalī, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta — each praised as ford-maker and elder, each reported as answering Ajātasattu off the point; they appear together in DN 2, DN 16, MN 30, MN 36, MN 77, SN 3.1, SN 44.9, Snp 3.6, the Vinaya (bowl episode) and the Milindapañha.

name: Śramaṇa and brāhmaṇa

definitions.definition: The two orders of religious men: the śramaṇa, who has gone forth, and the brāhmaṇa by birth and ritual; grammar gives 'śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa' as the type of perpetual enmity, and Aśoka finds both everywhere and urges concord between sects.
A true samaṇa or brāhmaṇa is made by conduct — calm, harmlessness, putting away evil — not by birth, shaving or rites.
One is a śramaṇa by equanimity, a brāhmaṇa by celibacy, and a brāhmaṇa or kṣatriya by deeds.

relations.note: the śramaṇa critique of sacrifice is one side of the contrast

notes: The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka already calls the wind-girdled Vedic seers śramaṇas (tea:taittiriya-aranyaka:2.7.1) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka mentions the śramaṇa (tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:4.3.22).

definitions.definition: Wanderers of all sects met in debating halls and parks to compare teachers; the reports of the six teachers come from such debate (SN 44.9, MN 36, MN 77, Snp 3.6).

name: The sixty-two grounds for views (Brahmajāla)

definitions.definition: All speculation about the past (18: eternalism 4, partial eternalism 4, finite/infinite 4, eel-wriggling 4, chance origin 2) and the future (44: percipient 16, non-percipient 8, neither 8, annihilation 7, nibbāna here and now 5) falls within sixty-two grounds; each is conditioned by contact and craving, and the Tathāgata knows them and what is beyond them.

relations.note: the Buddhist and Jain canons each catalogue all rival views, in different frames

notes: U36 owns the Brahmajāla Sutta; this unit supplies the view entries.

definitions.definition: Self and world are eternal, barren, pillar-firm — held on the evidence of meditative recollection of past lives or aeons, or by reasoning.
Some beings (Brahmā, gods not corrupted, the mind) are eternal, others not.
The world is finite, infinite, both or neither, from meditative perception or reasoning.
Self and world arose without cause, held by one who recalls only the arising of perception after life among the non-percipient gods, or by reasoning.
Sixteen forms of the view that the self survives death with perception.
Eight forms of the view that the self survives death without perception.

name: Neither percipient nor non-percipient after death

definitions.definition: Eight forms of the view that the self survives death neither with nor without perception.
Supreme nibbāna is enjoyment of the five sense pleasures, or one of the four absorptions.
(As reported) Fool and wise alike are annihilated at the breaking of the body; the person is made of four elements that return to their masses.
One of the sixty-two grounds (seven forms) and one of the two extremes avoided by the middle.
(As reported) Death is the end; the body burnt does not return.

relations.note: the Pali 'annihilation' and the Lokāyata 'no other world' state one position from two sides (death of the person / absence of a world beyond)

definitions.definition: (As reported) No gift, sacrifice, offering, fruit of deeds, this or other world, mother, father, spontaneously born beings, or ascetics who have realized the other world.
(As reported) Pāyāsi's view and experiments; the Isibhāsiyāiṃ's materialist statement.
(As reported) The doer does no evil and the giver gains no merit (Pūraṇa).
One of the four assemblies (84 kinds): deniers of action, for whom the world is barren and fixed.
Deeds, action and energy are effective; all Buddhas teach it; there is an element of initiative.
The true kiriyavāda: knowing self and world, influx and stopping, bondage and wearing away of karma.
(As reported) There is no cause or condition for defilement or purification, no effort; beings are transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature; all things are fixed.
A tenet that ends in inaction; the doctrine of cause (hetu) is the safe course; Makkhali's doctrine is the worst of all.
One-sided niyati is a wrong view; niyati with time, own-nature, deeds and effort is right view.

relations.note: in the Jain synthesis niyati is one of five co-causes

definitions.definition: (As reported) Every being, fool or wise, is purified simply by completing the fixed round of 8,400,000 great aeons; no vow or austerity can hasten it.
Rejected: purity does not come by transmigration.

name: The simile of the ball of string

definitions.definition: (As reported) As a ball of string thrown runs out unwinding to its end, so fool and wise run through saṃsāra to the end of suffering.

(As reported) Black, blue, red, yellow, white and supremely white classes of beings — from the cruel to the three Ājīvika leaders (AN 6.57, ascribed to Pūraṇa; DN 2, to Makkhali); in the Tamil report black, dark blue, green, red, golden, white, with release in the supremely white birth.
The Buddha's six: dark or bright birth leading to dark, bright, or neither-dark-nor-bright (nibbāna) results according to conduct.

relations.note: the classes are grades within the fixed round

definitions.definition: (As reported) The span of the fixed round of every being.

name: Makkhali's enumerations of births, karmas and worlds

definitions.definition: (As reported) 1,400,000 kinds of birth, 500 kinds of karma, 62 paths, 62 intermediate aeons, six classes, eight stages of a person, 4,900 kinds of Ājīvaka, 3,000 hells, 36 dust-realms, sevenfold wombs, gods, humans, goblins, lakes, knots, precipices and dreams — all within 8,400,000 great aeons.

name: Life and four kinds of atom (Tamil Ājīvaka)

definitions.definition: (Tamil report) Five principles: life (uyir) and four kinds of beginningless, indestructible, unchanging atoms (earth, water, fire, air) that combine into bodies and separate; a single atom is seen only by the divine eye.
(As reported) Earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and soul — unmade, barren, unmoving, not affecting one another; the sword passes between them.
(As reported) The same seven, eternal and uncuttable, joined to purification after 84 great aeons.
(As reported) Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla — the supremely white class, the only three the Ājīvikas recognize as having made an end, models of bodily austerity.

name: The six disācaras

definitions.definition: (Jain report) Six 'wanderers of the directions' who drew the eightfold Mahānimitta from the Pūrvas and shared it with Gosāla.

notes: Names recalled with low confidence; verify against Bhagavatī 15.

definitions.definition: (As reported) Nakedness, licking the hands, refusing food brought or prepared, eating at long intervals; fourfold 'fierce, severe' austerity, abstention from tasty food, restraint of the tongue; yet (Jain report) a rule allowing cold water, seeds, food made for the ascetic and women.

(Jain report) A soul may die and re-enter a body; Gosāla claimed to be Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa in his seventh re-entry; (commentators) the liberated soul of the Trairāśikas returns to saṃsāra through fondness for play.
(Jain report) A fiery power gained by severe austerity, with which Gosāla burnt two monks; turned against Mahāvīra, it returned upon Gosāla.
Countered by the cool power; its misuse is the downfall of the one who wields it.
(Jain report) Gosāla's lore of foretelling gain, loss, pleasure, pain, life and death.
A lore that sometimes fails and brings no release.
(Jain report) Gosāla's last drink, song, dance, salutation, the last storm-cloud, sprinkling elephant, battle of stones, and himself as last tīrthaṅkara — proclaimed around his death.
The Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ includes Maṅkhaliputta among the arhat seers and gives him a teaching on the steadfast protector who is not moved.

relations.note: a Jain text keeps a respectful saying of the teacher whose doctrine other Jain texts reject

definitions.definition: (Buddhist report) Nātaputta's teaching of restraint by all 'waters'.
(Jain account) Pārśva's law of four restraints, differing in form but not aim from Mahāvīra's five vows.
(As reported) Refusing every alternative on the other world, spontaneous beings, fruit of deeds and the Tathāgata after death.
Four grounds: fear of false speech, of grasping, of cross-examination; and dullness.

relations.note: Pali and Jain names for the refusal to affirm

definitions.definition: (As reported) The four topics on which Sañjaya refuses each of four alternatives: another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of good and bad deeds, the Tathāgata after death.
(Jain report) The assembly of the 'ignorant': 67 kinds; nothing about the soul can be known and knowing is useless — ignorance is better.
The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry or teach others; they are blind leading the blind.
(Jain report) The assembly of those for whom discipline or veneration alone is the way: 32 kinds.
All rival doctrines fall into four assemblies: action, non-action, ignorance, discipline.
180 kriyāvādins, 84 akriyāvādins, 67 ajñānikas, 32 vainayikas, derived combinatorially from the Jain categories and the candidate causes.

name: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga's review of rival doctrines

definitions.definition: Book 1 ch. 1 reviews in turn the five-element view, the one-self view, soul-is-body, the non-agent self, the self-as-sixth, the Buddhist momentary aggregates, destiny, ignorance, the doctrine of intention and the creation views, answering each; Book 2 continues with the lotus parable and Ārdraka's debates.

name: The five co-causes (kāla, svabhāva, niyati, pūrvakṛta, puruṣakāra)

definitions.definition: Time, own-nature, destiny, former deeds and effort: each held alone is wrong view, all together right view.
That all experience is due to past deeds, to God's creation, or to no cause; each ends in inaction.

name: The four negations of the holy life (MN 76)

definitions.definition: Annihilationism, non-action, no-cause, and seven bodies with the fixed round — each makes the holy life pointless.
Under a teacher who claims constant omniscience, an oral transmitter, a reasoner, or one dull and eel-wriggling.
Whether or not there is another world, one who holds that there is and lives well wins in either case; the denier loses in either case.

name: Claims and display of powers among the orders

definitions.definition: All six teachers claimed to be arahants with powers to win the sandalwood bowl; the Buddha forbade monks to display superhuman powers to lay people; the six teachers' contest of wonders ended in their rout.
(As reported) The soul is the body, bounded by the skin; it ends with the body; no soul can be drawn out of the body and shown.
Both 'soul is body' and 'soul is other than body' are extremes; the middle is dependent origination.
The soul is distinct from the body (Kesi's answer to Paesi).

relations.note: Jain and Brahmanical names for one identification of self with body

name: The body as the self (dehātmavāda)

definitions.definition: (As reported) The person is the body qualified by consciousness, known from 'I am fat, I am thin'.

notes: The Vedāntasāra's graded list (tea:vedantasara:refutation) distinguishes Cārvākas who take the gross body, the senses, the breath or the mind as the self.

definitions.definition: (As reported) Consciousness, absent in each element, arises in them when combined as a body — like intoxicating power — and perishes with them, like a drum's sound dying away.
(Jain report) From five elements a self arises and perishes with them.
Refuted: cognition arises only from prior cognition; mind is a beginningless continuum.
Refuted: consciousness is absent in the dead body; what experiences the elements is not one of them.

relations.note: no conscious survivor, so no other world

definitions.definition: (As reported) As the power to intoxicate arises from kiṇva, jaggery, dhātakī flowers and the like, none of which has it singly, so consciousness from the elements.
(As reported) There is no other world, because there is no one who goes there; no one returns from it.
The Lokāyatikas' denial is a wrong 'teaching of non-self'.

name: The materialists' experiments on the condemned

definitions.definition: (As reported) Sealing a criminal in a jar, weighing him alive and dead, cutting him open — no soul seen; answered with similes of dream, the hot iron ball, the conch and the fire-sticks.
(Jain report) Five kinds of denier — staff, rope, thief, partial, total.

name: The four elements as the only principles

definitions.definition: (As reported) Earth, water, fire and air are the principles; body, senses and objects are their aggregates; space is not counted.
(Jayarāśi) Stated only to reflect worldly belief; they too do not stand examination.

name: Perception the only means of knowledge

definitions.definition: (As reported) Only perception is valid; the world is as much as the senses reach.
(As reported) Pervasion cannot be established by any means; an adventitious condition cannot be excluded; inference proves either nothing new or nothing at all.
One who denies inference uses it in making his intention known.
Worldly inference is accepted; only inference to what transcends the worldly path is rejected.

relations.note: a narrower Lokāyata position than 'perception only'

definitions.definition: (Jayanta's report) Refined Cārvākas who hold the number of means of knowledge unfixable and grant a knower lasting as long as the body; distinct from the 'rogue' Cārvāka and the old teachers of bhūta-caitanya.
No means of knowledge can be defined without circularity; hence no object is established, not even the four elements; everyday practice goes on unexamined.
Even the knower of the highest follows the worldly path; there fool and wise are alike; practices are delightful while unexamined.
(As reported) The variety of things is from own-nature, not from an unseen cause or a creator.
One of five co-causes, wrong if held alone.

name: Pleasure as the aim of life

definitions.definition: (As reported) Live happily while life lasts; take pleasure as one takes the fish with its bones; what is past does not return.

name: Heaven, hell, lord and release in this world

definitions.definition: (As reported) Heaven is pleasure, hell is pain, the lord is the king, release is the death of the body.

name: The critique of sacrifice and funeral offerings

definitions.definition: (As reported) Sacrifice, śrāddha and the Veda are a livelihood of priests; the Veda was made by buffoons, knaves and demons.
Animal sacrifice, fire-worship and caste by birth are refuted; if the slain beast goes to heaven let brāhmaṇas slay brāhmaṇas.
(As reported) 'There is no gift, no sacrifice, no offering.'

relations.note: both the Lokāyata and the Buddhist Jātaka turn the sacrificed-animal argument against the brāhmaṇas

name: The Bārhaspatya view of the sciences

definitions.definition: (As reported) Only economics and government are sciences; the triple Veda is a cover for one who knows the course of the world.

name: The parable of the wolf's footprint

definitions.definition: (As reported) A man faked wolf-tracks to show how the learned mislead people with talk of unseen things.
